The *Vimānavatthu* (Stories of Mansions) is a collection of Buddhist texts describing the rebirths of individuals into celestial abodes (*vimānas*) as a result of their meritorious deeds. This particular section, the *Purisavimāna*, focuses on the rebirths of men. The *Pāyāsivagga* (Chapter on Pāyāsi) specifically recounts the story of King Pāyāsi, who, despite his great wealth and power, failed to perform acts of merit during his lifetime. After his death, he was reborn in a miserable state, while others who had given alms to the Buddha were reborn in magnificent mansions. The chapter serves as a moral lesson on the consequences of generosity and the importance of performing meritorious deeds. 1. The First Mansion of a Householder Just as the grove of variegated creepers shines forth—
the most excellent garden of the Thirty-three, supreme among them—
Just like that, this celestial mansion of yours stands illuminating the sky.
You have attained the power of a deva, O one of great majesty.
"What merit did you perform while being a human being?
By what means have you come to possess such blazing majesty,
and why does your complexion illuminate all directions?"
Thus that son of the gods,
being asked by Moggallāna, being pleased,
answered the question when he was questioned.
The fruit of which deed is this:
"Both I and my wife, while living as householders in the world of men, were like a well."
With a mind full of faith, we respectfully gave abundant gifts of food and drink; by that merit,
my complexion has become such as this.
"...and my radiance shines in all directions.
